transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-07-08 16:34 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Erin (VP VanguardPay), Derek (Staff ML), Rina (Security), Tom (PM)

Summary:
Quick POC scoping focused on workload characterization: QPS bursts, concurrency, input/output token distributions, tail-latency targets. Discussed benchmarks, data/sample payloads, network topology (VPC / Private), and compliance gating. Agreed on artifact exchange and scheduling a benchmark window.

Topics: workload pulse, tail-latency SLOs, batching/kv-cache, dedicated vs hosted, pilot timeline

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we can see the calendar, we'll go about 45 minutes, is that still good?
[00:06] Erin: yeah that's fine, thanks Maya. especially want to make sure we get the tail latency part nailed down — that's been our biggest problem in chat.
[00:11] Liam: cool, for context I'll be the SE pairing on this, i'll talk through the benchmarking approach and the config we'll need.
[00:17] Derek: just to set expectations, our current stack is a mix — inference calls to an internal microservice plus some third-party LLM access, typical QPS is 12 p50 but spikes to 180 qps during promos, concurrency is the hard bit because we see fat tails.
[00:29] Maya: okay that's useful. When you say spikes to 180 qps, over what burst window and what's average response length?
[00:34] Derek: bursts are generally 60-90s, avg prompt 85 tokens in, and outputs are variable, like 120 to 600 tokens depending on conversation depth. we also have some short intents ~20 tokens out.
[00:47] Tom: also note our mobile clients do a lot of small requests, like quick balance checks, high qps but low tokens. and the chat flows generate long outputs.
[00:56] Liam: great, that mix is exactly why we recommend capturing a traffic fingerprint — qps distribution, concurrency histogram, and token-length CDF for inputs and outputs. for the POC we usually ask for a 48 hour sample and a synthesized replay.
[01:10] Erin: ok, we can get logs. two questions though: what's the minimal dataset you need to get meaningful benchmark results, and how long will runs take?
[01:18] Maya: minimal is: representative intents (top 20), token length buckets, timestamped arrival times to model burstiness. baseline run we do for 1-2 hours at steady qps and then a few burst windows (5-10min, and 60-90s) to observe tail behavior. total lab time typically 3 hours but end-to-end process to analyze results is 2-3 days.
[01:36] Rina: security wise we need to confirm data residency and encryption — we can't send PII in plain text. will you need full payloads?
[01:44] Liam: you can anonymize tokens, we're mostly interested in length distributions and tokenization artifacts. sample inputs can be redacted, or we can use synthetic variants with identical token lengths. also we need network topology: are you planning to use Redwood Private in VPC or hosted?
[01:58] Erin: prefer Private in VPC for prod, pilot could be hosted if we get a dedicated pilot envelope. doesn't want to open everything up.
[02:06] Maya: understood. Pilot options: hosted pilot (fastest, but longer-term we recommend Dedicated pools or Private VPC for isolation). for tail-latency gating, Dedicated with pinned capacity helps avoid noisy neighbors.
[02:18] Derek: what's the difference in latency between hosted and dedicated typically?
[02:21] Liam: rough numbers — for similar model variants, hosted p95 might be 60-90ms higher in some regions because of multi-tenant queues and routing; Dedicated gives more predictable p99 under burst because of reserved capacity and less cross-customer batching. but exact numbers depend on model, quantization, and kernel selection.
[02:40] Speaker 1: i think you also have kv cache warmup effects — cold start can blow out your tail.
[02:44] Liam: yes exactly, kv cache and prefix caching reduce token cost and improve latency after warmup, but the first requests or new conversation keys will hit the cold path. we usually measure steady-state and cold-start separately.
[02:55] Tom: for our success criteria, product wants p95 < 350ms for short intents and p99 < 1.2s for long chat responses, plus throughput to handle 200 qps bursts without dropping requests. Is that realistic?
[03:08] Maya: it's reasonable as a target to shoot for with Dedicated/private deployments, but we'll need to model concurrency and token mix to validate. sometimes p99 is sensitive to output token lengths >400 tokens.
[03:19] Derek: how do you account for token distribution in benchmarks?
[03:22] Liam: we bucket by input token lengths and output token lengths and provide a replay that samples from that empirical distribution. also we replay arrival times to preserve burstiness and use variable concurrency clients to emulate real-world tails.
[03:34] Erin: you mentioned KV caching — can we control session affinity in the replay? our system pins users to shards which helps caches.
[03:41] Liam: yes, we can simulate affinity by pinning session IDs in the replay generator. that'll show the benefits of prefix/kv cache for repeated conversations.
[03:48] Maya: question on metrics: we will report p50/p95/p99 latencies, CPU/GPU utilization, GPU memory fragmentation, tokens/sec, and token cost per 1M tokens. Anything else you want?
[03:57] Derek: tail latency breakdowns per model layer would be amazing but i'm fine with per-request timeline and p99 breakdowns.
[04:04] Rina: for security audit we need packet-level egress info and KMS integration details. can you provide a diagram of how keys are managed and where logs are stored?
[04:12] Maya: yes, we'll attach our private deployment network diagram and an HSM/KMS integration note. that will be in the security pack we'll share.
[04:18] Erin: i want to clarify the benchmark pass/fail criteria — aside from latencies, what counts as a quality regression?
[04:25] Liam: we usually tie quality to a small eval set: top 50 prompts that must maintain a baseline LM score (ROUGE/quality proxies or human-validated check). if we see degredation in >5% of those prompts compared to your current baseline we'll flag it as a regression. we can use sampling or human review.
[04:45] Tom: for timeline, our execs want a pilot within 4 weeks. is that doable?
[04:49] Maya: yes if we get artifacts fast: traffic logs by 2026-07-14, Redwood will prepare harness and run first benchmark week of 2026-07-20. results review the following week.
[04:58] Speaker 1: what's the licensing/cost for a dedicated pilot?
[05:01] Maya: we'll send a pilot pricing sheet, typical reserved pilot covers dedicated GPU pool for 2-6 weeks, with uplift over hosted. i'll include cost estimates per 1M tokens and per-hour reserved.
[05:12] Derek: about quantization — do you recommend int8 for our models? some of our models are 13B-ish, we'd like to squeeze cost but not regress on quality.
[05:20] Liam: common approach is run A/B with fp16 baseline and int8/configured quantization. Redwood Optimize suggestions will recommend which tokens and sequences to quantize. we can measure quality delta on the eval set.
[05:31] Erin: compliance question — do we get audit logs for every inference? need that for our SOC2 evidence.
[05:36] Maya: yes both Dedicated and Private provide audit logs; retention can be configured. we'll include that in the security pack.
[05:43] Rina: one more: encryption in transit and at rest?
[05:45] Liam: TLS in transit and customer-managed KMS for Private deployments. At rest encryption uses KMS/HSM options.
[05:51] Derek: in terms of failure modes, do you have automatic fallback to smaller models if capacity is constrained?
[05:55] Maya: yes we support automatic fallback policies and region-level routing. for a POC we'll test fallback scenarios to observe latency and quality impact.
[06:02] Tom: can you simulate multi-tenant noise to see if we get tail spikes in hosted?
[06:06] Liam: we can introduce synthetic noisy workloads to measure interference on hosted, but that'll be more effort. for the pilot we'll compare hosted baseline vs dedicated with pinned capacity.
[06:16] Erin: ok that works. any blockers for us to share logs? personally we need a quick checklist of what can be redacted.
[06:22] Maya: checklist: remove user identifiers, keep tokenized lengths, preserve timestamps, include model name/hash if available, and mark any PII for redaction. we'll also accept synthetic payloads with equivalent token lengths if you prefer.
[06:36] Derek: side note, our infra uses service mesh and egress proxies which add ~40ms sometimes, should we subtract that when analyzing p99?
[06:43] Liam: we'll measure both application-side and infra-side latencies. in our reports we'll show measured e2e and also isolate Redwood service latency so you can subtract mesh overhead.
[06:53] Rina: on regulatory side, we may need a signed DPA — do you have a template?
[06:58] Maya: yes we'll include our DPA and standard SAs; legal will follow up if needed.
[07:04] Erin: fantastic. quick recap?
[07:07] Maya: recap — Redwood to share benchmark template, security pack, and pricing for a dedicated pilot by 2026-07-12. VanguardPay to send 48h traffic capture/redacted payloads and top prompts by 2026-07-14. Redwood to run first benchmark window week of 2026-07-20, then 30-min review. Success criteria: p95 < 350ms short intents, p99 < 1.2s long responses, handle 200 qps bursts. also run quality eval on top-50 prompts.
[07:35] Tom: agreed.
[07:36] Derek: yep, thanks.
[07:38] Rina: thanks, will follow up on compliance items.
[07:40] Maya: great, we'll send notes and links shortly. thanks everyone.

End of transcript.
